The command to take him as an enemy is an alert to exhausting one's full effort in fighting him and striving against him, as though he were an enemy who never tires and never falls short in waging war against the servant, counting every breath.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 35, verse 8:

How many are there who believe that they are the wronged party, entirely in the right in every respect, when the matter is not so; rather, there is with them a measure of truth and a measure of falsehood and wrongdoing, while with their opponent there is a measure of truth and justice. "Love of a thing makes you blind and deaf." A person is created with a natural disposition to love himself, so he sees only his good qualities, and he hates his opponent, so he sees only his bad qualities. Indeed, his love for himself may grow so intense that he sees his faults as virtues, as the Most High said: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good...?﴾

His hatred for his opponent may also grow so intense that he sees his virtues as faults, as it has been said:

*They looked with the eye of enmity, and had it been the eye of contentment, they would have found good what they found ugly.*

This ignorance is generally accompanied by desire and injustice, for man is indeed wrongdoing and ignorant.

Most of the religious practices of people are only customs they took from their fathers and forefathers, and imitated them in: affirmation and negation, love and hatred, allegiance and enmity.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 35, verse 10:

That is: whoever desires honour (al-'izza), let him seek it through obedience to Allah and His remembrance, through the good word and righteous deed.

In the supplication of qunut (du'a al-qunut, the supplication recited in the prayer): "Indeed, the one whom You befriend will never be humiliated, and the one whom You oppose will never be honoured."

Whoever obeys Allah has, by that, come under His protection (walaya) in respect of what he obeys Him in, and he has of honour in proportion to his obedience. Whoever disobeys Him has, by that, incurred His enmity (mu'adah) in respect of what he disobeys Him in, and he has of humiliation in proportion to his disobedience.

(Section)

Know that disobedience (ma'siyya) inevitably produces humiliation (dhull), for all honour lies in obedience to Allah the Exalted. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever desires honour—then to Allah belongs all honour﴾.

That is: let him seek it through obedience to Allah, for he will not find it except in obedience to Allah.

Among the supplications of some of the early generations (al-salaf) was: "O Allah, honour me through Your obedience, and do not humiliate me through Your disobedience."

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Even if mules prance with them and fine saddle-horses amble under them, the humiliation of disobedience does not depart from their hearts. Allah refuses except to humiliate whoever disobeys Him."

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said:

"I have seen sins deaden hearts, and persisting in them often brings humiliation.
Abandoning sins is the life of hearts, and for your soul, disobeying them is better.
Has anything corrupted religion except kings, and evil scholars and monks?"

(Subtle point)

Some of the early generations said: "People seek honour at the doors of kings, and they do not find it except in obedience to Allah."

And al-Hasan said: "Even if fine saddle-horses amble with them and mules prance with them, the humiliation of disobedience is truly in their hearts. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, refuses except to humiliate whoever disobeys Him. That is because whoever obeys Allah the Exalted has come under His protection, and whom Allah protects is not humiliated, as in the supplication of qunut:

"Indeed, the one whom You befriend will never be humiliated, and the one whom You oppose will never be honoured.""

(Section)

Reflect on the lesson in the fish, how it was created, and that it was created without limbs, because it has no need to walk, since its dwelling is water. It was not given lungs, because the benefit of the lung is breathing, and the fish has no need of it, since it is immersed in water. In place of limbs it was given strong fins, with which it propels itself from its two sides, as the boatman propels the vessel with oars from the two sides of the ship. It was clothed in a body covered with overlapping scales, interlocking like the coat of mail, to protect it from harms. It was given a strong sense of smell, because its sight is weak and the water veils it, so it smells food from afar and makes for it. It has been mentioned in some books on animals that there are passages from its mouth to its ear-openings, so it pours water in through its mouth and releases it from its ear-openings, and thereby it breathes, just as the land animal takes in cool breeze through its nose and then releases it to refresh itself. For water is to the sea animal what air is to the land animal. They are two seas, one more subtle than the other: the sea of air in which the land animal swims, and the sea of water in which the sea animal swims. If either kind were to leave its sea for the other sea, it would die. Just as the land animal suffocates in water, the sea animal suffocates in air. Glory be to Him whose signs the counters cannot enumerate, and whom no one can fully encompass in the detail of a single sign; rather, when they know one aspect of it, they are ignorant of other aspects.

Reflect on the profound wisdom in the fact that fish is the most prolific of animals, which is why you see in a single fish's roe an uncountable abundance of eggs. The wisdom behind this is that it should suffice for the many kinds of creatures that feed on it. Most of them eat fish, even the predatory beasts, for they crouch at the edges of thickets, lying in wait by clear water; when hunting on land becomes impossible for them, they watch for fish and snatch it. Since beasts eat fish, birds eat it, people eat it, large fish eat it, and land animals eat it, and God, glorified is He, has made it food for these kinds, His wisdom required that it be in this abundance. Had the servant seen what is in the sea of varieties of living creatures, jewels and kinds that none can count but God, and of which people know only a little, which bears no relation at all to what is hidden from them, he would have seen wonders, and would have known the vastness of God's dominion and the multitude of His hosts, which none knows but Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 35, verse 15 (part 1 of 3):

(O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy (15).)
In this verse, Allah, glory be to Him, makes clear that the need of His servants for Him is an intrinsic matter belonging to them, which never separates from them, just as His being Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy is intrinsic to Him. His self-sufficiency and His praiseworthiness are established for Him by His very essence, not by some cause that necessitated them. And the need of all others for Him is established for them by their very essence, not by some cause that necessitated it. Therefore this need is not to be explained by origination (huduth) or contingency (imkan); rather it is intrinsic to the one in need. The servant's need for his Lord is by his essence, not by a cause that made that need necessary, just as the self-sufficiency of the Lord, glory be to Him, is by His essence, not by some matter that made Him self-sufficient.
As Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said:
"Need is for me an attribute of my essence, constant forever, just as self-sufficiency is forever an intrinsic attribute of Him."
So the creation is needy and dependent upon its Lord by essence, not by a cause. Everything that is mentioned and established as a cause of poverty and need is rather evidence for poverty and need, not causes of it. For what is by essence is not caused; the poor one is by his essence in need of the self-sufficient one by His essence. Thus what is mentioned of contingency, origination and need are evidences of poverty, not its causes.
For this reason, the correct position on the question of why the world needs the Lord, glory be to Him, is other than the two views mentioned by the philosophers and the theologians (mutakallimun).
The philosophers said: the cause of need is contingency (imkan). The theologians said: the cause of need is origination (huduth).
The correct view: contingency and origination are mutually entailing, and both are evidence of need and dependence. The poverty of the world before Allah, glory be to Him, is an intrinsic matter that is not caused; it is poor by its essence before its Lord, who is self-sufficient by His essence.
Then one argues from its contingency, its origination, and other evidences for this poverty.
The point is that He, glory be to Him, informed about the reality and essences of the servants, that they are poor before Him, glory be to Him, just as He informed about His own sacred essence and reality, that He is Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy.
So absolute poverty from every aspect is established for their essences and realities as such, and absolute self-sufficiency from every aspect is established for the essence and reality of the Exalted as such. It is impossible for the servant to be other than poor, and impossible for the Lord, glory be to Him, to be other than self-sufficient, just as it is impossible for the servant to be other than a servant and for the Lord to be other than Lord.

(Admonition)
Among the most astonishing things is that you know Him yet do not love Him, that you hear His call yet delay in answering it, that you know the measure of profit in dealing with Him yet work for other than Him.
That you know the measure of His anger yet expose yourself to it, that you taste the pain of loneliness in disobeying Him yet do not seek intimacy in obeying Him.
That you taste the constriction of the heart when plunged into other than His speech, while speaking of Him, yet do not long for the expansion of the breast in remembering Him and conversing with Him.
That you taste torment when the heart clings to other than Him, yet do not flee from it toward the bliss of turning to Him and returning to Him in penitence.
And more astonishing than this is your knowledge that you will inevitably have Him, that you are most in need of Him of anything, while you turn away from Him and desire what distances you from Him.

(Chapter: On Allah being the Absolutely Self-Sufficient, and the creation being poor and in need of Him)
Allah, the Exalted, said: "O mankind, you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy."
In this verse Allah, glory be to Him, made clear that the poverty of the servants before Him is an intrinsic matter for them, never separate from them, just as His being Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy is intrinsic to Him. His self-sufficiency and praise are established for Him by His essence, not by a matter that caused them; and the poverty of all others before Him is established for them by their essence, not by a matter that caused it. So this poverty is not to be explained by origination or contingency; rather it is intrinsic to the poor one. The servant's need for his Lord is by his essence, not by a cause that necessitated that need, just as the self-sufficiency of the Lord, glory be to Him, is by His essence, not by a matter that made Him self-sufficient. As Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said:
"Need is for me an attribute of essence, constant forever, just as self-sufficiency is forever an intrinsic attribute of Him."
So the creation is poor and in need of its Lord by essence, not by a cause. Everything mentioned as a cause of poverty and need is evidence for poverty and need, not its causes, since what is by essence is not caused; the poor one by his essence is in need of the self-sufficient one by His essence. What is mentioned of contingency, origination and need are evidences of poverty, not its causes. Hence the correct position on the question of the cause of the world's need of the Lord, glory be to Him, differs from the two views mentioned by the philosophers and the theologians. The philosophers said: the cause of need is contingency; the theologians said: the cause of need is origination. The correct view is that contingency and origination are mutually entailing, and both are evidence of need and dependence. The world's poverty before Allah, glory be to Him, is an intrinsic matter that is not caused; it is poor by its essence before its Lord, who is self-sufficient by His essence. Then one argues from its contingency, its origination and other evidences for this poverty.
The point is that He, glory be to Him, informed about the reality and essences of the servants, that they are poor before Him, glory be to Him, just as He informed about His sacred essence and reality, that He is Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy. Absolute poverty from every aspect is established for their essences and realities as such, and absolute self-sufficiency from every aspect is established for the essence and reality of the Exalted as such. It is impossible for the servant to be other than poor, and impossible for the Lord, glory be to Him, to be other than self-sufficient, just as it is impossible for the servant to be other than a servant and the Lord other than Lord.

When this is understood, poverty is of two kinds:
A compelled poverty, which is a general poverty from which neither the righteous nor the wicked can escape; this implies neither praise nor blame, reward nor punishment, but is like the creature's being created and made.
The second is a chosen poverty, which is the result of two noble knowledges: one is the servant's knowledge of his Lord, and the second is his knowledge of himself. When these two knowledges are attained, they produce in him a poverty that is identical with his self-sufficiency, the sign of his success and felicity. People differ in this poverty according to their differing in these two knowledges. Whoever knows his Lord as absolutely self-sufficient knows himself as absolutely poor; whoever knows his Lord with perfect power knows himself with perfect weakness; whoever knows his Lord with perfect might knows himself with perfect humility; whoever knows his Lord with perfect knowledge and wisdom knows himself as ignorant. Allah, glory be to Him, brought the servant out of his mother's womb knowing nothing, unable to do anything, owning nothing, unable to give or withhold, to harm or benefit, or anything at all. So his poverty in that state before what sustains him was a visible, perceptible matter for everyone. And it is known that this belongs to him by the necessity of his essence, and what is by essence endures as long as the essence endures.
He has not moved from this rank to the rank of lordship and self-sufficiency; rather he has always been a servant, poor by his essence before his Creator and Originator.
Then when He bestowed His blessing upon him, poured out His mercy, and provided for him the means of his complete existence outwardly and inwardly, clothed him in the garments of His favor, gave him hearing, sight and heart, taught him, empowered him, directed him and moved him, enabled him to employ his fellow kind, subjected to him horses and camels, empowered him over the creatures of the water, drew birds down from the air, subdued the wild beasts, dug rivers, planted trees, split the earth, raised buildings, and devised means for his interests and guarded against what harms him, the wretched one imagined that he had a share of dominion, claimed for himself a kingdom alongside Allah, saw himself through other than that first eye, and forgot the state of nonexistence, poverty and need he had been in, until it was as if he had never been that poor needy one, but as if that were another person besides him.
As al-Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad, from the hadith of Bisr ibn Jahhash al-Qurashi, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once spat into his palm, placed his finger upon it, and said: "Allah the Exalted says: O son of Adam, how can you weary Me when I created you from the likes of this? When I had fashioned you and made you balanced, you walked between two cloaks, and the earth had its due from you. Then you gathered and withheld, until when the collarbones reached the throat, you said: 'I will give charity,' and when is the time for charity?"
From here some are forsaken and others are granted success. The forsaken one is veiled from his reality, forgets himself, forgets his poverty, need and dependence upon his Lord, so he transgresses, oppresses and rebels, and the wretchedness is fixed upon him. Allah, the Exalted, said: "Nay! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient" [Al-'Alaq: 6-7].
And He said: "As for him who gives and fears Allah and affirms the best, We will ease him toward ease. And as for him who is stingy and considers himself self-sufficient and denies the best, We will ease him toward hardship" [Al-Layl: 5-10].
So the most complete of creation are the most complete in servitude, and the greatest in witnessing their poverty, dependence and need of their Lord, and their not being self-sufficient of Him for the blink of an eye. For this reason, among his supplications was the Prophet ﷺ's saying: "Set right for me all my affairs, and do not leave me to myself for the blink of an eye, nor to anyone of Your creation." He also used to supplicate: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." He ﷺ knew that his heart is in the hand of the Most Merciful, the Mighty and Majestic, possessing none of it, and that Allah, glory be to Him, turns it as He wills; how could he not, when he recites the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "And had We not made you firm, you would almost have inclined toward them a little" [Al-Isra': 74].
So his ﷺ need of his Lord and his dependence upon Him was in proportion to his knowledge of Him, his nearness to Him, and his rank with Him. This is a matter that only appears from him to those after him as what seeps out from the outer vessel. For this reason he was the nearest of creation to Allah in means, the greatest of them in rank with Him, and the highest of them in station, because he perfected the station of servitude and poverty before his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. He used to say to them: "O people, I do not love that you raise me above my station; I am only a servant," and he said: "Do not praise me as the Christians praised Jesus son of Mary; I am only a servant, so say: the servant of Allah and His Messenger."

(Chapter: On the explanation of poverty and its degrees)
His saying: "The second degree: returning to the precedence by contemplating grace, which produces deliverance from seeing one's deeds, cuts off witnessing states, and purifies from the filth of contemplating stations." This degree is higher and loftier than the first, and the first is like a means to it. For in the first degree, through his poverty, he is emptied of worshipping anything other than his true Master, of wasting his breaths on other than His pleasure, of scattering his concerns on other than what He loves, and of preferring anything over Him in any state. This character and this conduct produce for him the purity of servitude, the cultivation of the secret between him and Allah, and sincere affection and love. He rises and retires with no concern but his Lord; his concern with his Lord has cut off all other concerns from him, his will has nullified all other wills, and his love for Him has erased from his heart every love for other than Him, as it was said:
"The heart was once captured every night by eighty, nay ninety souls and more.
He is infatuated with this one, then becomes attached to another, forgetting them all by the morning.
My heart was lost before your love, playing and frolicking in love of creatures.
But when your desire called my heart, it answered, and I see it never leaves your tent.
You have forbidden me hopes from you, if I am lying, and if I rejoice in the world with other than you.
And if there is anything in existence other than you that cools the wounded heart and delights it,
When the hands of desire play with your lovers, it has no way to slip from your door.
If estrangement from your homes overtakes it, your love remains within the breast and does not depart.
How many buyers among creatures have offered their hearts, yet see nothing fit but your love.
The desire for others is a blazing fire and a prison, and your love is Paradise, or wider still.
Alas for a heart attached to other than you, and alas for mercy upon what roams and toils."

Allah, the Exalted, has not made for a man two hearts within his body. Just as much as the heart receives concern, will and love, the concern, will and love opposing it leave it. It is one vessel with many drinks; whatever drink fills it leaves no room for another. A vessel fills with the finest drinks only when it finds it empty; but if it finds it full of something else, it does not dwell with it until what is in it leaves, and then it settles in its place, as one of them said:
"Her desire came to me before I knew desire, and found a heart empty, so it settled and took root."
So the poverty of the owner of this degree is emptying his vessel of every drink other than the drink of love and knowledge, for every drink that is other is intoxicating without doubt, and "what intoxicates in quantity is forbidden in small quantity." How far is the intoxication of desire and the world from the intoxication of wine! How can the drink of submission, which is the highest drink of the lovers, be placed in a vessel full of the wine of the world and desire, and he neither sobers from its intoxication nor recovers? Were this intoxication to leave the heart, it would fly on the wings of longing toward Allah and the Hereafter. But the wretched one was content with the base, and sold his share of nearness to Allah, knowledge of Him and His honor at the vilest price, a losing, cheated bargainer. He will know what share he lost when the lovers succeed and the falsifiers lose.

(Chapter: On the reality of poverty being the servant's turning with all his states to Allah)
When defilement by accidents is a fetter that binds hearts from journeying to the land of their life and bliss, which has no abode other than it, no rest but in it, no joy but in its dwellings, and no safety but among its people, then likewise the one whose heart has been touched by the spirit of devotion, who has tasted the sweetness of love and found intimacy in the fire of knowledge, has subtle inner accidents that fetter his heart from confronting the pure truth, from the soundness of need of it, from complete annihilation in it and enduring subsistence by its light, which is the goal of the journey and the path, the knowledge that the worshippers aim for, and around which the knowers circle. Everything that veils him or restrains the heart's sight and concern becomes a veil that blocks the arriving one, halts the wayfarer and turns back the seeker. Renunciation of it is therefore required for people of lofty resolve, as obligatory as a duty that cannot be avoided, like the renunciation of the traveler to the Hajj in the shades and waters he passes along the stations. The first fetters him from the realities by seeing accidents, the second fetters him from the ultimate ends by seeing states, so each fetters him from the sought goal, and this fetter results in not being able to pass through, which is a delayed and lagging loss.
When the servant knows this and its clarity is revealed to him, renunciation of states and poverty from them becomes obligatory upon him, just as renunciation of wealth and honor and emptying his heart of them is obligatory.

(Chapter: On dividing self-sufficiency into the high and the low)
Since poverty before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is itself the self-sufficiency in Him, the one most poor before Allah is the most self-sufficient in Him, the most humble before Him is the most honored by Him, the weakest before His hands is the strongest, and the most ignorant in his own estimation is the most knowing of Allah, and the one most hateful to himself is the nearest to the pleasure of Allah; as if mention of self-sufficiency in Allah along with poverty before Him are mutually entailing and correspondent, we shall mention a useful chapter on the high self-sufficiency.
Know that true self-sufficiency belongs only to Allah, the Self-Sufficient in His essence from everything other than Him. Everything other than Him bears the mark of poverty, just as it bears the mark of creation and making. Just as its being created is intrinsic to it, its being poor is intrinsic to it as already explained; its self-sufficiency is a relative, added, accidental matter, for it is self-sufficient only by an external matter, so it is self-sufficient by it and poor toward it. Absolute self-sufficiency is not attributed except to one whose self-sufficiency is a necessity of his essence; He is the Self-Sufficient in His essence from all else, the One, the Eternal Refuge, the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.
Self-sufficiency is of two kinds: a low self-sufficiency and a high self-sufficiency. The low self-sufficiency is self-sufficiency by borrowed, reclaimable things: women, sons, heaped piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle and tilled land. This is the weakest self-sufficiency, for it is self-sufficiency by a passing shade and a loan that soon returns to its owners; when they are gone, poverty remains entirely. As if self-sufficiency by them had been a dream that ended. No aspiration is weaker than the aspiration of one content with this self-sufficiency, which is a passing shade. This is the self-sufficiency of the people of the world, over which they compete, which they seek, and around which they circle; nothing is dearer to Satan and further from the Most Merciful than a heart full of love for this self-sufficiency and fear of losing it.
One of the early pious said: When Iblis and his hosts gather, they rejoice in nothing as they rejoice in three things: a believer who kills a believer, a man who dies in disbelief, and a heart in which there is fear of poverty. This self-sufficiency is enclosed between two poverties: a poverty before it and a poverty after it, and it is like a brief sleep between them.
Therefore it is fitting for the one who counsels himself not to be deceived by it nor make it the end of his pursuit, but when he attains it, to make it a means to his greater self-sufficiency and a path to it, and to make it a servant of his rather than his master. His soul should be too dear to him to enslave it to other than his true Master, or to make it a servant to another.

(Chapter: On high self-sufficiency)
As for high self-sufficiency, Shaykh al-Islam said: "It has three degrees. The first degree:

The strength of the heart: it is its freedom from the cause (of hardship), its acceptance of the decree, and its deliverance from dispute. The second degree is the strength of the soul (nafs), which is its steadfastness in what is desired, its freedom from (base) portions, and its clearing of ostentation (riya’).

The third degree is true richness, which has three stages. The first is witnessing His remembrance of you. The second is the constant contemplation of His pre-eternity (awwaliyyah). The third is triumph through His existence.

I say: It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Richness is not having abundant goods, but richness is the richness of the soul." When the soul becomes rich, the heart becomes rich. However, the Shaykh divided richness into these degrees according to its objects, and he said: "The strength of the heart is its freedom from the cause, its acceptance of the decree, and its deliverance from dispute." It is well known that this is a condition of richness, not richness itself. Rather, the presence of contention and dispute, and the absence of acceptance, is a barrier to richness. So this freedom and acceptance is a sign of the richness of the heart, not that its richness consists in them. The richness of the heart is only in the third degree alone, as will be explained, God willing. Richness becomes true only by attaining what fills one's poverty and removes one's need. In the heart there is great poverty, complete necessity, and intense need, which can be filled only by its triumph in attaining the Praiseworthy Rich One. If this is attained by the servant, everything is attained by him; and if it is missed, everything is missed. Just as He, glory be to Him, is the Rich in reality and there is no richness besides Him, so richness in Him is richness in reality, and there is no richness at all through anything else. Whoever is not made rich by Him from everything else, his soul will be consumed by sighs over other things; and whoever is made rich by Him, every sorrow leaves him and every joy and delight is present with him. And God is the One sought for help.

The Shaykh of Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) placed his discussion of the richness of the heart before the richness of the soul because the perfection of the soul's righteousness is its richness through uprightness in every respect, and its reaching the stage of tranquillity cannot occur except after the righteousness of the heart. It has been said that the righteousness of the soul precedes the righteousness of the heart, and there is much to be said about this, because the righteousness of each of them accompanies the righteousness of the other. But since the heart is the ruler, and its righteousness is the righteousness of all its subjects, it is more fitting that it be placed first. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily, it is the heart." When the heart becomes rich with what overflows upon it from the gifts and noble bounties of its Lord, it clothes the rulers and the subjects with robes fitting to them. It clothes the soul with the robes of tranquillity, serenity, contentment, and humble submission, so that it fulfils its duties with generosity rather than restraint, with openness, contentment, and eagerness. This is because the soul then becomes akin to the heart and agrees with it in most of its affairs, and their will becomes largely one; so it becomes for the heart a sincere vizier, after having been an open enemy. So do not ask what this support and agreement produce of tranquillity, pleasure of life, and bliss, which is a fraction of the bliss of the people of Paradise.

Yet the war between them has not laid down its burdens. Rather, its equipment and weapons lie hidden. Were it not for the strength of the heart's authority and its domination, the soul would fight with every weapon. Therefore, guarding the frontiers of the outer and inner self is an absolute duty for as long as the breaths of life last.

*And the war ends with praiseworthy consequences for the patient,
while the fleeing one is left with only regret.*

And the heart clothes the limbs with the robes of humility and dignity, the face with the robe of awe, light, and radiance, the tongue with the robe of truthfulness, sound and firm speech, and beneficial wisdom, the eye with the robe of reflection in looking and lowering the gaze from what is forbidden, and the ear with the robe of listening to advice and to beneficial speech that benefits the servant in his livelihood and his hereafter. It clothes the hands and feet with the robe of striving in acts of obedience wherever they are, with strength and power, and it clothes the private parts with the robe of chastity and guarding. So the servant rises and goes about, trailing these robes and dragging their hems and sleeves among the people.

Thus the richness of the soul derives from the richness of the heart and branches from it. When the heart is rich, its richness flows from it into the soul. The richness of the heart is what suits it: the realization in pure servitude, which is the greatest robe that can be bestowed upon it. Then it is rich by what this servitude requires for it of special knowledge, pure sincere love, what results for it from the effects of the sanctified attributes, and what those attributes require of rulings and servitudes connected to each attribute individually, and all of them together established in the Essence. This is a matter for which many volumes would be too narrow to explain. Indeed, the servant's portion of it, in knowledge and will, is like one who dips his finger into the sea; rather, the matter is greater than that. And God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, so valleys flow according to their measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17]. So when the heart is made rich by this richness, which is the ultimate of its poverty, the soul becomes rich in a way suited to it. The coldness that burdens it, its sluggishness, and its inclination toward the earth depart from it, and it acquires a warmth that causes it to move and become light in obedience and to seek the Highest Companion. Its coldness becomes directed toward its appetites, its portions, and its frivolities. Also the dryness that opposes its softness and its quickness of response and acceptance departs from it, for when it is dry and hard it is slow to respond and far from accepting, scarcely yielding. But when its coldness becomes warmth and its dryness becomes moisture, and it is watered with the water of life which God, Mighty and Majestic, sent down from the sky upon the hearts of His prophets, and made a resting place and a spring for it, and from it overflowed upon the hearts of their followers, and it caused to grow from every noble pair; then it submits to the rein of love toward its true Master, fulfilling its rights, standing by His commands, content with Him, and pleasing to Him in perfect tranquillity: ﴿O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾ [al-Fajr: 27–28].

(Section: On what enriches the heart and fills its poverty)

When the soul becomes free, good, and tranquil, rich with what its Owner and Originator has enriched it with, of the light which fell upon the heart and overflowed from it to the soul, it remains upright by that richness in the bestowed command, is preserved by it from the displeasing matter, and is cleared of ostentation. All of this depends on uprightness, inwardly and outwardly. For this reason the whole religion is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112], and He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain upright, no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 13].

This uprightness elevates the servant to the third degree of richness, which is richness in the Truth, blessed and exalted, above everything else, and it is the highest degree of richness. The first step of this degree is that you witness God's remembrance of you before your remembrance of Him, and that He remembered you among those of His creatures whom He remembered from the beginning, before your existence, obedience, and remembrance. He decreed your creation, provision, deeds, His kindness to you, and His blessings upon you, when you were not a thing at all. He remembered you, glory be to Him, with Islam, so He granted you success in it and chose you for it over those whom He forsook. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He named you "the Muslims" before﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. He made you fit for what you had never been fit for. It was He who made you fit through His earlier remembrance. Were it not for His remembrance of you with every beauty which He bestowed upon you, you would have had no path to Him. And who remembered you apart from Him with wakefulness, so that you awoke while others were in the sleep of heedlessness along with the sleepers? And who remembered you apart from Him with repentance, so that He granted you success in it, placed it in your heart, sent your motives toward it, and revived your sincere resolves for it, until you repented to Him and turned to Him, and you tasted the sweetness, coolness, and pleasures of repentance? And who remembered you apart from Him with His love, so that its flames stirred in your heart and its mounts turned toward Him, glory be to Him, and He filled your heart with His love after its long ruin, and made you intimate with His nearness after long loneliness and estrangement? He drew near to you first, so that you drew near to Him; then He rewarded this nearness with another nearness, so that your approach became surrounded by two of His nearnesses: a nearness before it and a nearness after it. Your love became surrounded by two of His loves: a love before it and a love after it. Your remembrance became surrounded by two remembrances: a remembrance before it and a remembrance after it. Were it not for His prior remembrance of you, none of that would have occurred, and no particle of His knowledge, His unity, His love, His fear, His hope, His reliance upon Him, His turning to Him, and His drawing near to Him would have reached your heart. All of these are effects of His remembrance of you. Then He, glory be to Him, remembered you with His successive blessings continuing according to the number of your breaths. For Him, in every blink of an eye and every breath, there are countless blessings by which He remembered you before your existence, made Himself known to you, and endeared Himself to you, although He is completely independent of you and of everything. This is merely His kindness, His grace, and His generosity, for He is the Generous, the Bountiful, the Benevolent by His very essence, not for exchange, nor for seeking reward from you, nor from need that impelled Him to it. How could that be, when He is the Rich, the Praiseworthy? So when even the slightest blessing from Him reaches you, know that He has remembered you by it. Let it be great in your sight because of His remembrance of you through it, for whoever remembers you with His kindness, begins with you in His goodness, and endears Himself to you with His blessing, has not belittled you. All of this is with His independence from you.

When the servant witnesses his Lord's remembrance of him, and that witnessing reaches his heart, it occupies him from everything else, and his heart attains a lofty richness that nothing resembles. This is like the slave who is never unremembered or forgotten by his master and teacher; he attains through his awareness of his master's remembrance of him a richness beyond his master's favours and noble gifts to him. This is the richness of God's remembrance of the servant. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, relating from his Lord, blessed and exalted: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it." This is a second remembrance after the servant's remembrance of his Lord, distinct from the first remembrance by which He made him a remembrer. The servant's awareness of both remembrances necessitates for him a richness beyond his Lord's favour and gifts to him. We have mentioned in the book *al-Kalim al-Tayyib wa'l-'Amal al-Salih* (The Good Word and Righteous Deed) among the benefits of remembrance: that it draws God's remembrance of His servant; and we have mentioned nearly a hundred benefits connected with remembrance, each of which has no parallel. It is a very beneficial book.

The point is that the servant's awareness and witnessing of God's remembrance of him enriches his heart and fills his poverty. This is in contrast to those who forgot God, so He caused them to forget themselves. Poverty in every good is theirs, and what they think is richness is among the greatest causes of their poverty.

(Section: Explaining the second degree of the degrees of richness in God, Mighty and Majestic)

The second degree of the degrees of richness in God, Mighty and Majestic, is the constant witnessing of His pre-eternity. This witnessing, according to the masters of the spiritual path (arbab al-suluk), is higher than what preceded it, and richness through it is more complete than the richness mentioned, because it is among the beginnings of richness in reality. When God opens to the servant's heart the witnessing of His pre-eternity, when there was nothing else, He being the true God, perfect in His names and attributes, Rich beyond everything else, Praiseworthy and Glorious in His essence, before He created anyone who would praise, worship, or glorify Him. He is worshipped, praised, living, self-subsisting; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, in pre-eternity and eternity. He has not ceased and does not cease to be described by the attributes of majesty and named by the names of perfection. Everything other than Him exists only through Him, and He, by His very Self, is not in need of another. He is the Self-Subsisting by whom everything subsists, and He has no need of anything else in His self-subsistence in any way.

When the servant witnesses His precedence in pre-eternity and the permanence of His true existence, and is absorbed by this from everything else of the originated things, then whoever did not exist is annihilated in His existence, as if he had never existed, and what has never ceased remains. The possible beings dissolve in His eternal, permanent existence, until they become like shadows which He extends, prolongs, and withdraws. The servant is made rich by this great witnessing, and nourished by it from his poverties and needs. This witnessing is considered by them to be superior to what preceded it, because the previous witnessing still contains a trace pointing to the servant's own existence. In this second witnessing, all existing things other than the First, the Exalted, are annihilated and perish in it, and become like their pre-eternity, which is non-existence. The pre-eternity of the Truth, blessed and exalted, has annihilated them. The servant remains a pure effacement and pure non-existence, even though his individual self is distinct and pointed to. But when it is ascribed to the pre-eternity of the Truth, Mighty and Majestic, it dissolves and perishes, and the One, the Truth, who has never ceased, remains. Thus everything other than the Truth, exalted is He, perishes in the servant's witnessing, as it perishes in itself. The servant then witnesses that everything other than God is vain, and that the manifest Truth is God alone. There is no doubt that richness through this witnessing is lasting, compared with the richness before it. This is not limited to the witnessing of His pre-eternity alone. Rather, the servant is made rich by every attribute of the Lord, majestic is His majesty, that appears to the hearts, in proportion to his share of knowing it and his fulfilment of its servitude.

Whoever witnesses the station of God's exaltation above His creation and His being above His servants, and His settling upon His Throne, as the most knowing of creation about Him, the truthful and believed, has informed him; and whoever worships according to the requirement of this attribute, so that his heart has a *samad* (a refuge) toward which the heart ascends, conversing with Him, lowering the gaze, standing before Him as the humble servant stands before a mighty King. He feels that his word and deed ascend to Him and are presented to Him along with the most intimate of His elect and friends; so he is ashamed that any word of his should ascend to Him that would disgrace and expose him there. He witnesses the descent of the divine command and decrees to the regions of the worlds at every moment, with all kinds of management and disposal: giving death and life, appointing and dismissing, lowering and raising, giving and withholding, removing and sending affliction, the turning of states, and the alternation of days among people, and other activities in the kingdom in which none acts but Him. His decrees are executed as He wills: ﴿He arranges the affair from heaven to earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Sajdah: 5]. Whoever gives this witnessing its due in knowledge and servitude is made rich by it.

Likewise, whoever witnesses the station of the all-encompassing knowledge, from which not an atom's weight escapes in the earth or in the heavens, nor in the depths of the seas, nor beneath the layers of the mountains; rather, His knowledge encompasses all of that in detailed knowledge; then he worships according to the requirement of this witnessing, guarding his thoughts, his will, all his states, his resolves, and his limbs. He knows that his outward and inward movements, his thoughts, his will, and all his states are manifest and uncovered before Him, open to Him, and nothing of them is hidden from Him. Likewise, when his heart is made aware of the attribute of His hearing, blessed and exalted, of the voices of His servants in their variety, whether loud or quiet, and that for Him there is no difference between one who speaks secretly and one who speaks aloud; the loudness of one who speaks loudly does not distract His hearing from the voice of one who speaks softly, nor does one hearing distract from another; the voices do not confuse Him in their multiplicity, variety, or combination, but all of them are to Him like one voice, just as the creation of all creatures and their resurrection are to Him like one soul.

Likewise, when he witnesses the meaning of His name, the All-Seeing, majestic is His majesty, who sees the crawling of the black ant on the solid rock in the darkest night, who sees the details of the creation of the tiny atom, its marrow, veins, flesh, and movement, and who sees the mosquito's wing spreading in the darkness of night; and when he gives this witnessing its due of servitude by guarding his movements and stillnesses, and is certain that they are in the sight of Him, blessed and exalted, and in a witnessing from which nothing is hidden from Him.

Likewise, when he witnesses the station of self-subsistence, which comprises the attributes of actions, that He is standing over everything, and standing over every soul for what it has earned; that He, exalted is He, is self-subsisting and sustains others, standing over them by His management, lordship, and domination, and bringing the reward of the doer of good to him and the reward of the doer of evil to him; and that by the perfection of His self-subsistence He does not sleep and it is not befitting for Him to sleep; He lowers the balance and raises it; the deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the night; sleep and slumber do not overtake Him, nor does He err or forget. This station is among the highest witnessings of the knowers, and it is the witnessing of Lordship.

The highest of these is the witnessing of Divinity (mashhad al-ilahiyya), which is the witnessing of the Messengers and their followers, the ḥunafāʾ (those who turn away from falsehood to pure monotheism). It is the testimony that there is no god but Him, and that the divinity of anything other than Him is false and impossible, just as the lordship of anything other than Him is likewise. None other than Him deserves to be taken as a god (yuʾallah) and worshipped, to have prayer and prostration offered to Him, and to deserve utmost love together with utmost humility, owing to the perfection of His names, attributes and actions. He alone is truly the one obeyed, the one alone worshipped, and to Him alone belongs judgment. Every servitude to other than Him is false, toil and error; every love for other than Him is a punishment to its bearer; every richness through other than Him is poverty and need; every honour through other than Him is abasement and lowliness; and every multiplicity through other than Him is scarcity and humiliation. Just as it is impossible for creation to have a lord other than Him, it is likewise impossible for them to have a god other than Him. He is the one to whom all desires end and toward whom all requests are directed. It is impossible that there be another god with Him, for the god in truth is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad), perfect in His names and attributes, the one to whom every creature's need is directed while He has no need of anyone, and by whom the existence of everything is sustained while His existence is not sustained by other than Himself. It is impossible that two such beings exist in existence; had there been two gods in existence, its order would have been corrupted in the greatest corruption and its arrangement disrupted in the greatest disruption. Just as it is impossible that He have two equal agents, each independent in action, for their independence negates each other's, and the independence of one prevents the lordship of the other. Thus the Tawhid of Lordship (tawḥīd al-rubūbiyya) is the greatest proof of the Tawhid of Divinity (tawḥīd al-ilāhiyya), and for this reason the Qur'an argues with it more than with anything else, due to the soundness and clarity of its indication, and the acceptance of intellects and natural dispositions (fiṭar) to it, and because the people of the earth acknowledge the Tawhid of Lordship. Likewise the idol-worshippers acknowledged it while denying the Tawhid of Divinity, saying: ﴿Has he made the gods one God?﴾ [Ṣād: 5], while acknowledging that God alone is the Creator of them, of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and that He alone possesses all of that. So God sent the Messengers to remind them of what their natural disposition contains of acknowledgement of His oneness, with no partner, and that if they returned to their natural dispositions and intellects, these would indicate the impossibility, impermissibility and falsehood of another god with Him. Thus the witnessing of Divinity is the witnessing of the ḥunafāʾ, and it is a witnessing that gathers the names and attributes. For this reason the name that signifies this meaning is the Name of God, majestic is His majesty, for this Name is the all-encompassing one. This is why all the Most Beautiful Names are attributed to Him, and one says: "al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, al-ʿAzīz, al-Ghaffār, al-Qahhār are among the names of God," and one does not say: "Allah is among the names of al-Raḥmān." God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And to God belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 180]. So in this witnessing all witnessings are gathered, and every other witnessing is only a witnessing of one of His attributes. Whoever's heart is broad enough for the witnessing of Divinity and fulfils its right of worship, which is the perfection of love together with the perfection of humility, glorification and the performance of the duties of servitude, then his richness is complete through the True God, and he becomes among the richest of servants. The state of such a person speaks:

"I have become rich without wealth, free of all people,
and true high richness is being free of a thing, not having it."

How magnificent is such richness, how great its worth and how exalted its rank! Kingdoms shrink before it and whatever lies below them, and in comparison to it they become like a shadow cast by the one who casts it, or like a phantom visiting in a dream, which the imagination brings and waking from sleep dispels.

(Section: On explaining the third degree of richness in the Lord)

The third degree of richness in the Lord, majestic is His majesty, is attaining His existence (al-fawz bi-wujūdih). This richness is the highest degree of richness, because the first and second richnesses were effects of remembering God and turning towards Him. From the sincerity of turning towards Him there overflowed onto the heart lights of the sanctified attributes, the heart became rich by that, and there also arose the lights of awareness of His sufficiency for His servant, the goodness of His trusteeship, and His self-subsistence through His management and the goodness of His management, so the soul also became rich by that. As for this third richness, which is richness in the Real, it is from the effects of the existence of the Reality (ḥaqīqa), and it occurs only after ascending from the effects of the attributes to the effects of the existence of the Essence (dhāt). This existence comes after the unveiling of the certainty of the eye (ʿayn al-yaqīn), when the dawn of Tawhid rises. This is its beginning and its perfection at the rising of its sun, so the mist of perishing existence is dispelled and the sun of enduring existence shines, and every mist is dispelled before it. This is an expression of a light cast into the heart, by which the greatness of the Essence is unveiled, just as by the light before it the greatness of the attributes was unveiled. If a trace of the attributes of the Essence or the attributes of actions makes the heart and soul rich, what then do you think of what the spirits are unveiled to of the lights of the holiness of the Essence, characterised by majesty and generosity? This is a richness that description cannot attain and that does not come under explanation, so the poor servant becomes rich by the existence of his Master, the Mighty, the Merciful. How wondrous is a poverty that ends, and a richness that endures, and a life sweeter than desire! So do not consider yourself incapable of reaching this station, for between you and it lies sincere seeking; it is only a true resolve and the uprising of a free person who has a worth and value in his own soul, and who is jealous for it lest he sell it for something base. It has come in a divine report (athar ilāhī) in which God, Mighty and Majestic, says: "O son of Adam, I created you for Myself, so do not play; and I have taken charge of your provision, so do not weary yourself. O son of Adam, seek Me and you will find Me; for if you find Me you will find everything, and if you miss Me you will miss everything, and I am more beloved to you than everything." So whoever seeks God sincerely finds Him, and whoever finds Him, His existence makes him independent of everything, and he becomes free, rich, and held in awe, with His lights and radiance upon his face. And if his Master, majestic is His majesty, escapes him, what he hopes for recedes far and his toil lengthens. Whoever attains this richness has his eye comforted by everything, because his eye has been comforted with God and by attaining His existence; and whoever does not attain it has his soul broken into sighs over the world. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever wakes up with the world as his greatest concern, God will put his poverty before his eyes, scatter his affairs, and nothing from the world will come to him except what has been decreed for him. And whoever wakes up with the Hereafter as his greatest concern, God will place his richness in his heart, gather his affairs for him, and the world will come to him humbled, and God is swifter to every good toward him." This is true poverty and true richness. If this is the richness of one whose greatest concern is the Hereafter, then how much more so is it for one whose greatest concern is God, Mighty and Majestic. This is by way of alerting and a fortiori.

(Section: On mentioning sayings of the people of the path concerning poverty and richness)

Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: "Poverty is that you are not made rich by anything other than God; its sign is the absence of all causes."

I say: He means their absence in relying upon them and being at peace with them; rather, they become nothing in comparison to the priority of their Causer and His singular eternity.

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Farghānī was asked about needing God, the Exalted, and being made rich by Him, and he said: "When the need for God, the Exalted, is sound, being made rich by Him is sound; and when being made rich by Him is sound, the need for Him is sound. So it cannot be said which of them is more perfect, for neither is complete without the other."

I say: Being made rich by God is the very same as poverty toward Him, and they are two expressions of one meaning, for the perfection of richness in Him is the perfection of His servanthood, and the reality of servanthood is the perfection of need for Him from every aspect, and this need is the very richness in Him. So there are not two things here to seek the preference of one over the other; rather, they are imagined as two things only according to what one is free of and what one is needy of. They are one reality and one station, called "richness" in relation to its emptiness from perishing existents, and "poverty" in relation to the narrowing of its aspiration and its gathering upon God, the Mighty and Majestic. It is an aspiration that travels away from a thing and connects to another; its travel away from others is richness, and its travel toward God is poverty. When it arrives at Him, it becomes rich in Him through the perfection of its poverty toward Him, since after arrival it has another poverty, different from its first poverty, and its poverty is only perfected by this arrival.

Ruwaym was asked about poverty and said: "Releasing the soul into the rulings of God, the Exalted." I say: If he means the religious ruling, it is correct; but if he means the cosmic, decreed ruling, this statement is not accurate without detail, as its explanation has already been given. Releasing the soul into His rulings that He dislikes and hates, and releasing it into His rulings that must be opposed and resisted by His other rulings, is a departure from servanthood.

It was said: "The poor man has three characteristics: guarding his secret, performing his obligation, and protecting his poverty."

I say: Guarding the secret is keeping it hidden, a protection for it from others and a jealousy over it lest it be revealed to one who does not know it or cannot be trusted with it. Performing the obligation is standing by the right of servanthood. Protecting poverty is preserving it from the stain of dwelling with others, and guarding it from every cause that would spoil it, and concealing it as far as one can. Ibrāhīm ibn Adham said: "We sought poverty and richness met us; people sought richness and poverty met them."

Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh was asked about richness and said: "It is security in God, the Mighty and Majestic." Abū Ḥafṣ was asked: "With what should the poor man come before his Lord?" He said: "The poor man should come before his Lord with nothing but his poverty."

Some of them said: "Indeed, the sincere poor man fears richness, lest it enter him and spoil his poverty for him, just as the greedy rich man fears poverty, lest it enter him and spoil his richness for him." Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith said: "The best of stations is holding firmly to patience in poverty until the grave."

I say: From here the poet said:

"They said: 'Tomorrow is the feast; what will you wear?' I said: 'A robe, its hem dragging in wide...'
Poverty and patience are two garments beneath which lies a heart that sees the bond of feasts and gatherings.
Time is mourning for me if you are absent, O my hope; and the feast is as long as you are before my sight and my hearing."

Ibn al-Jalāʾ was asked: "When does the poor man deserve the name of poverty?" He said: "When no remnant of himself remains in him." It was said to him: "How is that?" He said: "When he has something, he has nothing; and when he has nothing, it is his."

I say: The meaning of this is that no remnant of his self remains upon him. If he belongs to himself, he does not belong to his Lord, and he has lost its right and wasted its happiness and perfection. But if he does not belong to himself and all of him belongs to his Lord, he has secured every portion for himself and attained his soul's felicity, for if he belongs to God, God belongs to him; and if he does not belong to God, God does not belong to him, so how could his self belong to him? This is of those who have lost their souls.

It was said: "The reality of poverty is that the poor man does not become rich in his poverty through anything except the One to whom his poverty is directed."

Abū Ḥafṣ said: "The best means by which a servant draws near to his Master is the constant need for Him in all states, the continual adherence to the Sunna in all actions, and seeking sustenance from a lawful source."

Some of them said: "The poor man should not let his aspiration outrun his step."

I say: This points to his aspiration being attached to the obligation of his present time, and that his aspiration does not transgress the obligation of the time before completing it. It also points to shortening his hope, and that his aspiration is not attached to a time he does not reckon of reaching. It also points to gathering his aspiration upon guarding the time, and not weakening it by dividing it among times.

It was said: "The least that is required of the poor man in his poverty are four things: knowledge that guides him, scrupulousness that restrains him, certainty that carries him, and remembrance that comforts him." Abū Sahl al-Khashshāb said to Manṣūr al-Maghribī: "It is only poverty and humiliation." Manṣūr said: "Rather, it is poverty and honour." Abū Sahl said: "Poverty and dust (thará)." Manṣūr said: "Rather, poverty and the Throne (ʿArsh)."

I say: Abū Sahl pointed to the beginning, and Manṣūr to the end.

Al-Junayd said: "When you meet the poor man, meet him with gentleness and do not meet him with knowledge, for gentleness comforts him and knowledge makes him lonely." I said: "O Abū al-Qāsim, how can a poor man be made lonely by knowledge?" He said: "Yes; the poor man, when he is sincere in his poverty, if knowledge is cast upon him, melts as lead melts in fire."

Abū al-Muẓaffar al-Qarmīsīnī said: "The poor man is the one who has no need of God."

Abū al-Qāsim al-Qushayrī said: "This expression has a slight ambiguity for one who hears it, as though it indicates heedlessness of the aim of the people. Its speaker only intended the dropping of demands, the absence of choice, and contentment with what God, Glorified and Exalted, makes flow."

I say: Furthermore, it is an unsound and erroneous statement, for the needs of this servant toward God are as numerous as his breaths, since his need is not like the needs of others who have portions and shares; rather, their needs in comparison to this servant's need are like a drop of spittle in a sea. His need of God in every blink of an eye is that He preserve his state for him, establish his heart, raise him through the stations of servanthood, turn away from him what would spoil them, make him know the stages of the path, its hiding places and its times, make him know the places of His pleasure so he may do them and resolve upon them, and the places of His wrath so he may resolve to abandon them and avoid them. What needs could be more numerous or greater than these? So the correct statement is: the poor man is the one whose needs of God are as numerous as his breaths or more. The servant has, in every breath, every moment and every blink of an eye, many needs of God of which he is not aware. The neediest of people toward God is the one who perceives these needs and seeks them from their source and by their path. If it is necessary to apply that expression at all, it is to say: he is the one who has no need of God that conflicts with His good pleasure and lowers him from the station of servanthood to the level of self-sufficiency. As for saying "he has no need of God," it is an ugly ecstatic utterance (shaṭḥ).

As for Abū al-Qāsim's interpretation of the statement as dropping demands, the absence of choice, and contentment with the courses of destiny, this is only good in some states, concerning the decree that runs over him without his choice, and which he is not commanded to repel or resist with another decree, as has already been explained.

But if he is commanded to repel it and resist it with a decree that God loves more—and this is commanded either as obligation or as recommendation—then dropping demands, the absence of choice in it, and abandoning striving are the very essence of incapacity, and God blames incapacity.

Ibn Khafīf said: "Poverty is the absence of possessions and the exit from the rulings of attributes." I say: He means the absence of attributing anything to oneself as ownership, and that one exits the rulings of one's own soul's attributes and replaces them with the rulings of the attributes of one's Owner and Master. An example: one exits the ruling of the attribute of one's power and choice, which requires claiming ownership, disposal and attributions, and remains under the rulings of the eternal attribute of need, which requires incapacity, poverty and dependence, as in the prayer of istikhāra: "O God, I seek Your good counsel by Your knowledge, and I seek Your power by Your power, and I ask You of Your great bounty, for You are capable and I am not capable, You know and I do not know, and You are the Knower of the unseen." This is the servant's being characterised by the rulings of the sublime attributes and his exit from the rulings of the attributes of the soul.

Abū Ḥafṣ said: "Poverty is not valid for anyone until giving is more beloved to him than taking. Generosity is not that the one who has give to the one who lacks; generosity is that the one who lacks gives to the one who has."

Some of them said: "The poor man is the one who sees no need for himself of any thing except his Lord, blessed and exalted." Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh was asked: "When does the poor man find rest?" He said: "When he sees for himself no time other than the one he is in." Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir said: "Among the rulings of the poor man is that he should have no desire; and if he must have some, his desire should not exceed what suffices him." Someone was asked about the sincere poor man and said: "He who neither possesses nor is possessed."

Dhū al-Nūn said: "Lasting poverty toward God together with mixing is more beloved to me than lasting purity together with self-admiration. And God knows best."

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 35, verse 22:

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And you cannot make those in the graves hear﴾, the context of the verse shows that what is meant is that the dead disbelieving heart cannot be made to hear in a way that benefits from it, just as those in the graves cannot be made to hear in a way that benefits them. He, glorified is He, did not intend that the people of the graves hear nothing at all. How could that be, when the Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that they hear the sound of the sandals of those who follow the funeral procession?

He also informed us that the slain of Badr heard his speech and address, and he prescribed the greeting of peace upon them in the form of direct address to one who is present and hears, and he informed us that whoever greets his believing brother with peace, the brother returns the greeting.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 35, verse 28 (part 1 of 2):

So the scholars, through knowledge of Him and of His command, are the people of His fear (khashyah). The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the most knowledgeable of you about Allah, and the most fearful of Him."

(Section)

Al-wajal (trembling), al-khawf (fear), al-khashyah (awe-fear) and al-rahbah (dread) are closely related terms, not synonyms. Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd said: Fear (khawf) is the anticipation of punishment at every passing breath.

It has been said: Fear is the agitation and movement of the heart from remembering the one feared.

It has been said: Fear is the strength of knowledge of the paths of the rulings; this is the cause of fear, not fear itself.

It has been said: Fear is the heart's flight from the arrival of what is disliked, upon sensing it.

Al-khashyah is more specific than fear, for khashyah belongs to the knowers of Allah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. Thus it is fear joined with knowledge. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the most God-fearing of you, and the most fearful of Him."

Fear is movement, while khashyah is contraction, constriction and stillness. One who sees an enemy, a flood or the like has two states: the first is movement to flee from it, which is the state of fear; the second is his stillness and settling in a place where it cannot reach him, which is khashyah. From this comes "khasha al-shay'" (the thing became fearful/receded), and the doubled and the weak-lettered forms are siblings, like "taqaddda al-bazi" and "taqaddaḍa."

As for al-rahbah, it is the excess of fleeing from what is disliked, and it is the opposite of al-raghbah (desire), which is the journey of the heart in pursuit of what is desired.

Between al-rahab (dread) and al-harab (flight) there is correspondence in form and meaning, joined by al-ishtiqaq al-awsat (the "middle derivation"), which is the arrangement of the permutations of a root around one comprehensive meaning.

As for al-wajal, it is the pounding of the heart and its splitting open at the mention of one whose authority and punishment are feared, or at seeing him.

As for al-haybah (awe), it is a fear combined with veneration and reverence, and it is most often accompanied by love and knowledge. Al-ijlal (majesty-reverence) is veneration joined with love.

So fear belongs to the generality of believers, khashyah belongs to the knowing gnostic scholars, haybah belongs to the lovers, and ijlal belongs to those brought near. The degree of fear and khashyah corresponds to the degree of knowledge and gnosis, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed I am the most knowledgeable of you about Allah, and the most fearful of Him." In one narration it reads "khawfan" (fear). He also said: "If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, and you would not take pleasure in women on the beds, and you would go out to the high ground, crying out to Allah the Exalted."

The one who fears seeks refuge in flight and restraint; the one who has khashyah seeks refuge in holding fast to knowledge. Their likeness is that of one who has no knowledge of medicine and that of the skilled physician: the first seeks refuge in diet and avoidance, while the physician relies on his knowledge of medicines and diseases.

Abu Hafs said: Fear is the whip of Allah, with which He straightens those who stray from His door. He also said: Fear is a lamp in the heart, by which one sees what is in it of good and evil. Every single thing, when you fear it, you flee from it, except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for when you fear Him, you flee to Him.

So the one in fear flees from his Lord to his Lord.

Abu Sulayman said: Fear has never left a heart without its ruin. Ibrahim ibn Sufyan said: When fear settles in hearts, it burns the places of desire within them and drives worldliness out of them. Dhu al-Nun said: People remain on the path as long as fear has not departed from them; when fear departs from them, they lose the path. Hatim al-Asamm said: Do not be deceived by a righteous place, for no place is more righteous than Paradise, and Adam encountered there what he encountered. Do not be deceived by abundance of worship, for Iblis, after long worship, met what he met. Do not be deceived by abundance of knowledge, for Balam ibn Ba'ura met what he met, and he knew the Greatest Name. Do not be deceived by meeting and seeing the righteous, for no person was more righteous than the Prophet ﷺ, yet his enemies and the hypocrites gained nothing from meeting him.

Fear is not sought for its own sake; rather it is sought for something else, as a means. For this reason it departs when the feared thing departs, for the people of Paradise have no fear upon them, nor do they grieve.

Fear relates to actions, while love relates to the Essence and the Attributes. For this reason the love of believers for their Lord multiplies when they enter the abode of bliss, and no fear reaches them there. This is why the station and rank of love is higher and loftier than the station and rank of fear.

Praiseworthy, sincere fear is that which stands between its bearer and the prohibitions of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If it exceeds that, what is feared from it is despair and hopelessness.

Abu Uthman said: The sincerity of fear is abstinence from sins, outwardly and inwardly.

[Section: Who is the knowledgeable possessor of the truth?]

Know that consensus (ijma'), proof (hujjah) and the great multitude (al-sawad al-a'zam) are the knowledgeable possessor of the truth, even if he is alone, and even if the people of the earth oppose him. 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi said: I accompanied Mu'adh in Yemen, and I did not part from him until I buried him in the dust in Syria. Then after him I accompanied the most jurisprudent of people, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and I heard him say: "Hold to the community (al-jama'ah), for the hand of Allah is with the community." Then one day I heard him say: "Rulers will be set over you who delay the prayer from its appointed times, so pray the prayer at its proper time; it is the obligatory prayer, and pray with them, for it is a supererogatory prayer for you." He said: I said, "O companions of Muhammad, I do not know what you are narrating." He said: "What is it?" I said: "You command me to the community and urge me toward it, then you tell me: pray the prayer alone, it is the obligatory one, and pray with the community, it is supererogatory." He said: "O 'Amr ibn Maymun, I had thought you were among the most jurisprudent people of this town. Do you know what the community is?" I said: "No." He said: "The majority of the community are those who have departed from the community. The community is what agrees with the truth, even if you are alone." In another wording: he struck my thigh and said: "Woe to you! Most people have departed from the community, and the community is what agrees with the obedience of Allah, the Exalted."

Nu'aym ibn Hammad said: When the community becomes corrupt, then hold to what the community was upon before it became corrupt, even if you are alone, for then you are the community. Al-Bayhaqi and others mentioned it.

One of the imams of hadith, when the great multitude was mentioned to him, said: "Do you know what the great multitude is? It is Muhammad ibn Aslam al-Tusi and his companions." Thus those who differ were transformed, those who were made the great multitude, the proof and the community, and they were the majority; they made them a measure for the Sunnah, made the Sunnah an innovation, and the recognized (ma'ruf) an abomination, because of the paucity of its people and their isolation across eras and regions. They said: "Whoever deviates, Allah will make him deviate into the Fire." The ones who differ did not know that the deviant (al-shadhdh) is one who opposes the truth, even if all people are upon it except one of them, for then it is they who are the deviants.

Indeed all people deviated in the time of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, except a small group; they were the community. The judges, the jurists, the caliph and his followers were all the deviants, while Imam Ahmad alone was the community. When this did not sit well with people's minds, they said to the caliph: "O Commander of the Faithful, will you and your judges, your governors, your jurists and your scholars all be upon falsehood while Ahmad alone is upon the truth?" His knowledge did not stretch to accommodate that, so he seized him with whips and punishment after a long imprisonment. There is no god but Allah! How alike is this night to the previous one! This is the clear path of the people of the Sunnah and the community until they meet their Lord, which their predecessors walked and their successors await: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with Allah; of them is one who has fulfilled his vow, and of them is one who awaits, and they have not altered in the least﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23]. There is no power and no strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

(Section)

Ikrimah said: "All blood is ignorance, and what clarifies this is His saying: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾."

And whoever fears Him and obeys Him by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions is a knower, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord? Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾

A man said to al-Sha'bi: "O scholar!" He replied: "We are not scholars; the scholar is only one who fears Allah."

Ibn Mas'ud said: "Sufficient is the fear of Allah as knowledge, and reliance on being deluded by Allah as ignorance."

His saying ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge truly fear Allah﴾ implies restriction from both sides: that none fear Him except the knowers, and that none is a knower except one who fears Him. So none fears Him except a knower, and every knower fears Him. When knowledge is absent, khashyah is absent; and when khashyah is absent, it indicates the absence of knowledge. But error occurs regarding the meaning of the knowledge necessarily tied to khashyah, for one supposes it can be attained without it, and this is impossible. In nature, one who truly knows the fire, the lion and the enemy, and faces them, does not fear them? And one who throws himself from a height does not fear death? His security in these situations is evidence of his lack of knowledge, and at best he has a supposition that does not reach the rank of certain knowledge.

If it is said: this is refuted by Iblis's disobedience, for it was from knowledge, not ignorance; and by His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾; and He said: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign﴾; and He said of Pharaoh's people: ﴿They denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾; and He said: ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud—and it has become clear to you from their dwellings. Satan made their deeds appear fair to them and barred them from the way, though they were discerning﴾; and Moses said to Pharaoh: ﴿He said: You know that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights﴾; and He said: ﴿And Allah would not mislead a people after He has guided them until He makes clear to them what they should beware of﴾; and He said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their own sons﴾, meaning the Qur'an or Muhammad ﷺ; and He said: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?﴾; and He said: ﴿They do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾. Denial (juhud) is rejecting the truth after recognizing it, and this is frequent in the Qur'an?

It is said: The proofs of Allah do not contradict one another; rather they are all truth, each confirming the other. Since He, glorified be He, has affirmed ignorance for one who does evil, while that person has acknowledged Him, His messenger, and that He forbade that and threatened punishment for it, yet He still judges him to be ignorant, which is the reason he did evil, then how about one who associates others with Him, disbelieves in His signs and opposes His messengers? Is that not the most ignorant of the ignorant?
